name: Neapolitan pizza
summary: A soft, blistered, wood-fired pizza topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil.
story: Flatbreads with toppings have long existed around the Mediterranean, but pizza as we know it grew up among the working poor of 18th and 19th century Naples, who ate it as cheap street food. The tomato topping became common after tomatoes arrived from the Americas. A popular story says the Margherita was made for Queen Margherita of Savoy in 1889, using the colours of the Italian flag; historians doubt parts of that tale. In 2017 UNESCO recognised the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo as intangible cultural heritage.

origin_claims.claim: Pizza developed as street food in Naples and spread worldwide with Italian emigration.
The Margherita was created in 1889 for Queen Margherita, using red, white and green toppings.

name: Tagliatelle al ragù
summary: Ribbons of fresh egg pasta in a slow-cooked meat sauce, the dish that spaghetti bolognese is loosely based on.
story: Bologna's ragù is a slow-simmered sauce of beef and pork, a little tomato, soffritto vegetables, milk and wine. It is served with fresh egg tagliatelle rather than spaghetti, a pairing that holds the sauce well. The Accademia Italiana della Cucina registered a reference recipe in Bologna in 1982, and the dish shows how seriously the region treats its food traditions. Outside Italy the dish became spaghetti bolognese, which differs considerably from the original.

origin_claims.claim: The meat sauce is documented in Italian cookbooks from the late 19th century, including one by Pellegrino Artusi.
A reference recipe was deposited with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce by the Accademia Italiana della Cucina in 1982.

name: Arancini
summary: Golden fried rice balls filled with ragù, peas and cheese, from Sicily.
story: Arancini ("little oranges") are rice balls coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried. The dish is connected with the period of Arab rule in Sicily, when rice and saffron arrived on the island, though the breadcrumb-coated version is probably later. Palermo and Catania argue over the name and shape: in the west they are arancine and round, in the east arancini and cone-shaped. They are traditionally eaten on 13 December, the feast of Saint Lucy, when bread and pasta are avoided in some places.

origin_claims.claim: Linked to Arab-era Sicily, when rice and saffron were introduced.
Palermo and Catania disagree on whether they are feminine (arancine, round) or masculine (arancini, conical).

name: Risotto alla milanese
summary: Creamy saffron risotto finished with butter and Parmesan, the classic companion of braised veal shank.
story: Risotto alla milanese gets its yellow colour from saffron and is made with butter, stock and the short-grain rice grown in the Po valley. A well-known legend says a glassmaker's apprentice added saffron to a wedding feast at the Milan cathedral in the 16th century, since saffron was used to colour glass. That story is very likely a legend, and the first written recipes only appear in the 19th century. It is the traditional accompaniment to ossobuco.

origin_claims.claim: A glassmaker's apprentice added saffron to rice at a 1574 wedding feast during the building of Milan Cathedral.
Written recipes appear in 19th century cookbooks.

name: Chiacchiere
summary: Thin, crisp ribbons of fried dough dusted with icing sugar, made for Carnevale.
story: Chiacchiere ("chatter") are strips of enriched dough, fried until blistered and crisp, then dusted with icing sugar. The idea of fried carnival pastry goes back to ancient Rome, where similar sweets, sometimes called frictilia, were cooked in lard during winter festivals; a direct line to the modern pastry is hard to prove. Every region has its own name for them, including frappe in Lazio, cenci in Tuscany, bugie in Piedmont and crostoli in the north-east.

origin_claims.claim: Descended from fried dough sweets made at Roman festivals.

name: Ribollita
summary: A thick Tuscan soup of white beans, dark kale and other vegetables, thickened with stale bread and served reheated.
story: Ribollita means "re-boiled": the soup is made one day, left to rest, and brought back to the boil the next, when the beans, vegetables and bread have melted together into a dense, spoonable stew. It belongs to the frugal cooking of rural Tuscany, where stale unsalted bread, beans and winter greens such as cavolo nero were everyday food. Many cooks finish it with a thread of raw olive oil, and some layer it with sliced onion in a pot and bake it. A popular tale says it grew out of leftovers gathered after the feasts of wealthy households; that explanation is hard to verify and is best read as a story.
origin_period: Medieval to early modern, as a peasant dish

origin_claims.claim: A soup of bread, beans and winter vegetables was everyday rural food in Tuscany, reheated over several days.
It began as a way for servants to reuse the leftovers of their masters' feasts.

name: Spaghetti alla carbonara
summary: Spaghetti coated in a silky sauce of egg, aged pecorino cheese, cured pork cheek and black pepper, with no cream.
story: Carbonara is a Roman pasta built from just a few ingredients: guanciale (cured pork jowl), eggs, pecorino romano and plenty of black pepper. The heat of the freshly drained pasta cooks the eggs into a creamy sauce rather than scrambling them, which is the technique that matters most. Cream, garlic and onion are not part of the traditional recipe. The name is usually linked to charcoal (carbone) but nobody knows for sure why. The dish is not found in Italian cookbooks before the middle of the 20th century, so older origin stories should be treated with caution.

origin_claims.claim: The earliest printed recipes appear in the years after the Second World War, so the dish seems to be a relatively modern one.
It was invented in Rome when Allied soldiers brought bacon and eggs that cooks combined with pasta.
It was a meal of charcoal burners (carbonari) in the Apennines.

name: Orecchiette with turnip tops
summary: Little ear-shaped pasta tossed with bitter turnip greens, garlic, chilli and anchovy, a signature of Puglia.
story: Orecchiette ("little ears") are made from durum wheat semolina and water, shaped by pressing and dragging small pieces of dough with the thumb. They are strongly associated with Puglia, especially Bari and the area around it, where they are often sold fresh in the street. The classic sauce uses cime di rapa, the leafy shoots of a bitter brassica, softened with garlic, chilli and salted anchovy in olive oil. The pairing of eggless pasta and vegetables fits the traditional cooking of southern Italy, which relied on local greens and grain. The exact age of the shape is unclear.

origin_claims.claim: Orecchiette are a traditional hand-shaped pasta of Puglia, made from durum wheat and water.
The shape originated in the Middle Ages in the Apulian countryside, with some stories pointing to Angevin-period Puglia.

name: Panettone
summary: A tall, airy yeast-raised Christmas cake from Milan, studded with raisins and candied citrus peel.
story: Panettone is a domed, soft-crumbed sweet bread enriched with butter and egg yolks and full of raisins and candied orange and citron. Traditional versions are leavened with a long-fermented sourdough starter, which gives the loaf its light texture and keeps it fresh for days. It is closely tied to Milan and to the Christmas season, and industrial production in the 20th century spread it across Italy and beyond. Several origin stories circulate, involving a nobleman, a baker named Toni, or a cook who rescued a burnt dessert; these tales are fun but not supported by documents, and the cake's medieval roots as an enriched Christmas loaf are better established.
origin_period: Medieval origins, modern form 19th to 20th century

origin_claims.claim: An enriched Christmas bread has been made in Milan for centuries, and the modern tall form developed with commercial bakeries.
It was named after a baker called Toni, whose bread (pan de Toni) was a happy accident.

name: Pandoro
summary: A buttery, golden star-shaped Christmas cake from Verona, dusted with vanilla icing sugar.
story: Pandoro ("golden bread") is a soft, fruitless yeast cake rich in eggs and butter, baked in a distinctive eight-pointed star mould and dusted with icing sugar so it looks like a snowy mountain. It is associated with Verona and the Veneto and, like panettone, is a staple of the Italian Christmas table. Industrial bakers in Verona made it widely available from the late 19th century. Its ancestry is debated: some link it to older Veronese Christmas breads such as nadalin, and others to rich Austrian or Venetian sweet breads.
origin_period: Late 19th century in its modern form

origin_claims.claim: The modern pandoro was developed and commercialised by bakers in Verona in the late 19th century.
It descends from older Veronese Christmas breads such as nadalin.
It derives from Venetian or Austrian enriched breads served to the nobility.
